'''Paul Robert Chernoff''' (21 June 1942,  [[Philadelphia]] – 17 January 2017)<ref>biographical information from ''American Men and Women of Science'', Thomson Gale 2004</ref>  was an American mathematician, specializing in functional analysis and the mathematical foundations of quantum mechanics.<ref name=ObitSFC>{{cite news|title=Obituary. Paul Chernoff|newspaper=San Francisco Chronicle|date=2 April 2017|url=http://www.legacy.com/obituaries/sfgate/obituary.aspx?pid=184707211}}</ref> He is known for Chernoff's Theorem, a mathematical result in the Feynman path integral formulation of quantum mechanics.<ref>{{cite journal|author=Butko, Yana A.|title=Chernoff approximation of subordinate semigroups and applications|journal=Stochastics and Dynamics|volume=18|issue=3|pages=1850021|year=2015|doi=10.1142/S0219493718500211|arxiv=1512.05258|s2cid=119146783}}</ref> He was also the author of [[Limerick (poetry)|limericks]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=[the] Musical Reimagings of the Limericks of P. Chernoff, by Speed Killvirus |url=https://neweveningisle.bandcamp.com/album/the-musical-reimagings-of-the-limericks-of-p-chernoff |access-date=2025-03-30 |website=New Evening Isle Inc. |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Limericks by P. Chernoff |url=https://math.berkeley.edu/~chernoff/limericks.html |access-date=2025-03-31 |website=math.berkeley.edu}}</ref>

==Education and career==
Chernoff graduated from [[Central High School (Philadelphia)|Central High School in Philadelphia]]. He matriculated at [[Harvard University]], where he received bachelor's degree, ''[[summa cum laude]]'', in 1963, master's degree in 1965, and Ph.D. in 1968 under [[George Mackey]] with thesis ''Semigroup Product Formulas and Addition of Unbounded Operators''.<ref>{{MathGenealogy|id=30697|name=Paul Robert Chernoff}}</ref>

At the [[University of California, Berkeley]], he became in 1969 a lecturer, in 1971 an assistant professor, and in 1980 a full professor. U. C. Berkeley awarded him multiple Distinguished Teaching Awards and the Lili Fabilli and Eric Hoffer Essay Prize.<ref name=ObitSFC/> In 1986 he was a visiting professor at the [[University of Pennsylvania]].

Chernoff was elected in 1984 a Fellow of the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]]<ref>{{cite news|newspaper=University of California Bulletin, week of August 6–10, 1984|volume=33|issue=3|title=American Association for the Advancement of Science Elects University Members|year=1984|page=12|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=2vM2AQAAMAAJ&pg=PA12}}</ref> and in 2012 a Fellow of the [[American Mathematical Society]].

He gave in 1981 a simplified proof of the [[Hilbrand J. Groenewold|Groenewold]]-[[Léon Van Hove|Van Hove]] theorem,<ref>Chernoff, Mathematical obstructions to quantization, Hadronic J., vol. 4, 1981, pp. 879–898</ref><ref>{{cite book|author=Sternberg, Shlomo|authorlink=Shlomo Sternberg|author2=Guillemin, Victor|authorlink2=Victor Guillemin|title=Symplectic Techniques in Physics|publisher=Cambridge University Press|year=1990|pages=101–102|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=O7Rbx4ptxqsC&pg=PA101|isbn=9780521389907}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|author=Berndt, Rolf|title=Einführung in die Symplektische Geometrie|publisher=Vieweg|year=1998|pages=119–120|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=BXOMdQ-jFUsC&pg=PA119|isbn=9783322802156}}</ref> which is a [[no-go theorem]] that relates classical mechanics to quantum mechanics.<ref name=ObitSFC/>
